Hypothesis (data-grounded answer): Original papers in Experimental Economics are much longer than original papers in Psychology. In this replication dataset, the average original paper in Experimental Economics (project 'ee', n = 18 papers) is 28.0 pages (median 27.5, SD 7.37, range 16–45), whereas the average original paper in Psychology (Reproducibility Project: Psychology, project 'rpp', n = 95 unique papers after deduplication by title) is 11.2 pages (median 9, SD 6.35, range 1–31). That is, Experimental Economics originals average roughly 2.5 times the length of Psychology originals — about 17 pages longer (28.0 vs 11.2). The conclusion is robust to the unit-of-analysis choice: deduplication changes the rpp mean by only 0.01 pages (11.23 deduplicated vs 11.22 row-level, n=95 vs 97). This aligns with disciplinary convention: economics journals (e.g., American Economic Review) publish full-length articles, whereas the psychology originals in RPP largely come from short-article outlets (e.g., Psychological Science, JPSP), explaining the systematically shorter length.

Workflow executed: (1) loaded data/meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv (927 rows × 57 columns; length fully complete, no missing values); (2) subset project=='ee' (18 rows, 18 unique ids/titles, verified 1 row per paper) and project=='rpp' (97 rows, 97 unique ids, 95 unique titles); (3) computed mean/median/SD/min/max of length per group, deduplicating rpp by title as the primary estimate and keeping the row-level mean as a check; (4) verified that length is constant within every id and title, and quantified the deduplication effect (2 rows dropped, mean shift 0.01 pages). Script and output saved as analysis artifacts.
